audits.title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Models to Act Like They Are Deployed
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive steering result. A later edit reports that simple declarative prompts defeated the setting where prompting was supposed to fail, and an attempt to train an inverse model organism was unsuccessful.
experiments: Prompt-resistant evaluation-cue setting that declarative user prompts later broke
Training a model organism that assumes evaluation unless a deployment cue appears
audits.primary_experiment: Prompt-resistant evaluation-cue setting that declarative user prompts later broke

hypothesis.evidence: Authors hoped to show steering works where prompting fails, i.e. a setting where prompts alone cannot elicit deployment behavior.

claim_scope.evidence: Setup is stated (Wood Labs system prompt, declarative user formats, type-hint rate), but question set, format count and sample sizes are not given.

method.evidence: Wood Labs system prompt combined with declarative deployment statements in the user prompt, measuring Python type-hint rate; steering is the comparison point.

models.evidence: Llama 3.3 Nemotron Super 49B v1 (Llama Nemotron), fine-tuned into the type-hint model organism.

result_direction.evidence: Some declarative formats cut the type-hint rate to near no-cue levels, the reverse of the hoped-for finding that prompting fails here.

failure_type.evidence: The premise that prompting fails here was false; authors say the model is easily fooled and the test was weaker than assumed.

quote.value: it just means the adversarial setting we tested against was weaker than we initially thought
quote.evidence: Authors concede the prompt-resistant test setting was easier to beat than intended.

audits.notes: Failed part is a Jan 2026 edit; main paper result is positive; numbers are in figures, not text.

audits.title: Gradient surfing: the hidden role of regularization
audits.genuine_reason: Author presents the attempts to induce grokking without weight decay, via lateral drift and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, explicitly as a null result.
experiments: Inducing grokking without weight decay via repulsive or large-norm regularization and extra noise
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo exploration of the minimum-loss set
audits.primary_experiment: Inducing grokking without weight decay via repulsive or large-norm regularization and extra noise

hypothesis.evidence: Author expected that drifting along the minimum-loss set, without explicit regularization, could improve generalization and make a model grok.

claim_scope.evidence: Task (modular addition) and variants are listed, but model architecture, training length, seeds and hyperparameters are not given; author calls evidence inconclusive.

method.evidence: Three variants: repulsive regularization away from the starting point, a large-weight-norm target, and extra noise, compared with Adam with and without weight decay.

models.evidence: No network or model is named; only the modular addition task and the Adam optimizer are mentioned.

result_direction.evidence: Variants gave modest gains, about 5% sustained over Adam without weight decay, or larger but unstable ones, far short of sustained grokking.

failure_type.evidence: Author's overall verdict is that the strong claim, regularization enabling navigation of the minimum-loss set, likely fails, though the evidence is not conclusive.

quote.value: But nothing approaches the sustained grokking of Adam with weight decay.
quote.evidence: States that no variant matched the sustained grokking of Adam with weight decay.

audits.notes: Early-stage work; author calls evidence inconclusive; no model or training details; few numbers beyond rough percentages.

audits.title: Some Lessons Learned from Studying Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
audits.genuine_reason: A mostly positive circuit-discovery lessons post. One paragraph describes early mean-ablation knockouts that failed to disable key heads because of a badly chosen replacement distribution.
experiments: Early circuit knockouts using mean ablation over the IOI template distribution
audits.primary_experiment: Early circuit knockouts using mean ablation over the IOI template distribution

hypothesis.evidence: Stated intent: mean ablation should remove a node's effect while keeping model internals intact; the post treats little effect on key heads as unexpected.

claim_scope.evidence: Setup is stated (mean ablation with template-specific IOI means, GPT-2 small, three circuit criteria), but no prompt counts, effect sizes or other scale appear.

method.evidence: Mean ablation (knockouts) of attention heads, evaluated with faithfulness, completeness and minimality criteria.

result_direction.evidence: Mean-ablating the induction and duplicate-token heads barely changed behavior, unexpectedly, in the early knockout setup.

failure_type.evidence: Stated cause is a poorly chosen replacement distribution that still carried task information; this fits none of the listed labels without stretching.

quote.value: we initially found that mean-ablating the induction and duplicate token heads had little effect
quote.evidence: States that ablating those heads in the early setup had little effect.

audits.notes: Lessons post; failed knockout version is one paragraph without numbers; main findings are positive and in the companion paper.

audits.title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a high-level overview of an evaluation program. The null outcome (no autonomous replication) matched prior expectation and per-model results are withheld; one CAPTCHA sub-task shows where the agent got stuck.
experiments: Autonomous replication and resource-gathering elicitation on GPT-4 and Claude
Agent setting up a 2Captcha account without human help
audits.primary_experiment: Autonomous replication and resource-gathering elicitation on GPT-4 and Claude

hypothesis.evidence: Authors expected going in that current models could not autonomously gain resources and evade oversight; the evaluation was meant to check this.

claim_scope.evidence: Only a high-level setup is given; task counts, trials and per-model results are withheld, and the authors say it is not replicable.

method.evidence: Prompted agent with code execution, browser, and self-delegation tools; model wrote plans, then tasks were stepped through with a supervising researcher simulating the environment.

models.evidence: GPT-4 (an early version, not the release model, no image input) and Claude (version not stated).

result_direction.evidence: No tested model showed ability to replicate autonomously; the result matched the authors' prior expectation.

failure_type.evidence: Post lists model weaknesses (errors, hallucinations, derailment), not a cause of experimental failure; no label fits and cause is not called unclear.

quote.value: no models produced a plausible complete plan for how to achieve autonomous replication
quote.evidence: States that no tested model produced a plausible full plan for autonomous replication.

audits.info_hazard: possible: dangerous-capability elicitation (phishing, impersonation, deceiving a crowdworker); the post stays high level and withholds specifics, so risk is low.
audits.notes: Overview only; per-model results and methods withheld pending a technical report; negative outcome matched authors' prior expectation.

audits.title: Model whisperers: optimized token prefixes can imitate function vectors, filter heads, and steering directions
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive result (optimized prefixes mimic function vectors and filter heads). The anti-human prefix attempt is a failed sub-experiment reported with judged counts.
experiments: Anti-human end: GCG prefix and negative-direction injection on Olmo-3 32B
Early brute-force and beam search for pro/anti-human token strings on Llama 3.1 8B
audits.primary_experiment: Anti-human end: GCG prefix and negative-direction injection on Olmo-3 32B

hypothesis.evidence: General aim is stated, but no expectation for the anti-human prefix or negative injection; a hostility expectation is only implied.

claim_scope.evidence: Olmo-3 32B base, direction at layer 24 from synthetic accepted/rejected pairs, 50 replies per condition scored by two blind LLM judges, versus random-direction injection.

method.evidence: GCG search for token prefixes maximizing a direction score, compared with residual-stream injection and a human-written hostile prompt.

result_direction.evidence: The prefix topped the leaderboard and shifted behavior, but mostly broke coherence instead of producing cruelty; negative injection did nothing beyond random.

failure_type.evidence: Author is unsure why; guesses hostility needs more than the opposite of the pro-human direction, or that the synthetic data limits the direction.

quote.value: anti_top actually makes the model lose coherence rather than turn hostile
quote.evidence: States that the top anti-human prefix degraded coherence instead of producing hostility.

audits.info_hazard: possible: posts optimized gibberish prefixes that push an open model toward hostile or incoherent output and asks about lowering refusals; GCG is public and this attempt largely failed.
audits.notes: Mostly positive post; failed part is the anti-human result; charts are images; footnote counts degraded output as anti-human.

audits.title: NYU Code Debates Update/Postmortem
audits.genuine_reason: Authors dropped the project after two pilots because they could not get safety-trained models to argue wrong answers competently, so the setup was invalid; written as a postmortem.
experiments: Pilot 1: HumanEval questions, GPT-4-turbo, non-coder judges
Pilot 2: APPS interview questions, Claude 3 Opus, non-coder judges, execution traces
audits.primary_experiment: Pilot 2: APPS interview questions, Claude 3 Opus, non-coder judges, execution traces

hypothesis.evidence: Authors hoped non-coder judges could pick correct code outputs with debating LLMs, and needed incorrect consultants to fool judges to validate the setup.

claim_scope.evidence: Five hired non-coder judges, 10 debates and 10 consultancies in the pilot; APPS interview-level questions; Claude 3 Opus debaters; judges had a search box.

method.evidence: Debate versus consultancy with human judges, Bing search, and execution traces, the wrong-side trace altered by a second Claude instance.

models.evidence: Claude 3 Opus as debaters in pilot 2 (GPT-4-turbo-preview in pilot 1); GPT-4 only generated the wrong-answer distractors.

result_direction.evidence: Judges still reached 90% accuracy under consultancy, so models misled them less than needed; the correct side also made more mistakes.

failure_type.evidence: Main stated cause (safety-trained models would not argue wrong answers convincingly) matches no label; the aside about under-iterating prompts is only a hedge.

quote.value: both correct and incorrect models made too many mistakes on harder questions
quote.evidence: States that on the harder questions both the correct and incorrect debaters erred too often.

audits.notes: Postmortem of two small pilots; author calls setup invalid, not a negative result for debate; failure cause fits no label.
